question: The corpus contains both the 2019 ratified RISC-V specification (version 20191213) and the 2025 Unprivileged ISA manual (version 20250508). Which should control an answer about the current definition of a base integer instruction such as JALR, and how may the 2019 edition still be used?

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged Architecture (version 20250508)
results.text:
2.5. Control Transfer Instructions | Page 31

The indirect jump instruction JALR (jump and link register) uses the I-type encoding. The target
address is obtained by adding the sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate to the register rs1, then setting
the least-significant bit of the result to zero. The address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) is
written to register rd. Register x0 can be used as the destination if the result is not required.

Plain unconditional indirect jumps (assembler pseudoinstruction JR) are encoded as a JALR with rd=

x0. Procedure returns in the standard calling convention (assembler pseudoinstruction RET) are
encoded as a JALR with rd=x0, rs1=x1, and imm=0.

The term call is used to refer to a JAL or JALR instruction with a link register as destination, i.e., rd≠x0.
Conventionally, the link register is x1 or x5. A call using JAL or C.JAL is termed a direct call. A C.JALR
expands to JALR x1, 0(rs1) and is a call. A call using JALR or C.JALR is termed an indirect-call.

The term return is used to refer to a JALR instruction with rd=x0 and with rs1=x1 or rs1=x5. A C.JR
instruction expands to JALR x0, 0(rs1) and is a return if rs1=x1 or rs1=x5.

The term indirect-jump is used to refer to a JALR instruction with rd=x0 and where the rs1 is not x1 or x5
(i.e., not a return). A C.JR instruction where rs1 is not x1 or x5 (i.e., not a return) is an indirect-jump.

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged Architecture (version 20250508)
results.text:
Note that the JALR instruction does not treat the 12-bit immediate as multiples of 2

          bytes, unlike the conditional branch instructions. This avoids one more immediate
          format in hardware. In practice, most uses of JALR will have either a zero immediate
          or be paired with a LUI or AUIPC, so the slight reduction in range is not significant.

          Clearing the least-significant bit when calculating the JALR target address both
          simplifies the hardware slightly and allows the low bit of function pointers to be used
          to store auxiliary information. Although there is potentially a slight loss of error
          checking in this case, in practice jumps to an incorrect instruction address will
          usually quickly raise an exception.

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA (document version 20191213)
results.text:
This HINT encoding has been chosen so that simple implementations can ignore HINTs altogether, and instead execute a HINT as a regular computational instruction that happens not to
    mutate the architectural state.

RVC HINTs do not necessarily expand to their RVI HINT counterparts. For example, C.ADD x0, t0
might not encode the same HINT as ADD x0, x0, t0.

    The primary reason to not require an RVC HINT to expand to an RVI HINT is that HINTs
    are unlikely to be compressible in the same manner as the underlying computational instruction.
    Also, decoupling the RVC and RVI HINT mappings allows the scarce RVC HINT space to be
    allocated to the most popular HINTs, and in particular, to HINTs that are amenable to macro-op
    fusion.

args.answer:
**The 2025 manual controls.** For any question about what a base integer instruction *is* today — including JALR — the controlling text is *The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged Architecture*, document version 20250508. It defines JALR as the indirect jump using the I-type encoding, where "the target address is obtained by adding the sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate to the register rs1, then setting the least-significant bit of the result to zero," and "the address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) is written to register rd," with x0 usable as the destination when the result is not required [1]. This edition is the current one because it incorporates "all ratified extensions through February 2025" and removes unratified content, such as the earlier sketch of the RV128I base ISA [2]. Its own commentary also carries the current rationale: JALR does not treat the 12-bit immediate as multiples of 2 bytes (unlike conditional branches), and clearing the least-significant bit of the target "allows the low bit of function pointers to be used to store auxiliary information" [3]. The current vocabulary built on JALR — call (JAL/JALR with a link register destination, conventionally x1 or x5), return (JALR with rd=x0 and rs1=x1 or x5), and indirect-jump (JALR with rd=x0 and rs1 not x1/x5) — is likewise stated in the 2025 manual [4].

**How the 2019 edition (20191213) may still be used — for history and comparison only, never as the current rule:**

1. *Ratification status and version lineage.* Prefaces reproduced in the 2019-era text record that at that time "no parts of the standard have been officially ratified," with modules labeled Ratified, Frozen, or Draft [5], and that the base integer ISA version number was incremented to 2.1 to reflect the ratified RVWMO memory model and the exclusion of FENCE.I, counters, and CSR instructions from the earlier base ISA [9]. This is useful for explaining *why* the definition changed, not for stating what it now is.
2. *Design rationale and change notes.* The 2019 edition preserves the reasoning behind JALR's shape — e.g., that JALR was defined so a LUI plus JALR pair can reach any 32-bit absolute address, and AUIPC plus JALR any 32-bit PC-relative range [6] — and its change list notes a modification of the implicit hinting suggestion on JALR to support more efficient macro-op fusion [5].
3. *Corroboration and older assembler conventions.* The 2019 pseudoinstruction table lists `jr rs` as `jalr x0, 0(rs)`, `jalr rs` as `jalr x1, 0(rs)`, and `ret` as `jalr x0, 0(x1)` [7]; the 2025 manual instead describes plain unconditional indirect jumps (JR) as JALR with rd=x0 and returns (RET) as JALR with rd=x0, rs1=x1, imm=0 [1], while the draft assembly manual uses the `jalr x0, rs, 0` operand order [10]. Similarly, C.JALR is described in both editions as performing the same operation as C.JR plus writing pc+2 to x1, expanding to `jalr x1, 0(rs1)`, valid only when rs1≠x0, with the rs1=x0 code point being C.EBREAK [8]. Agreement between editions is corroborating only; where the two differ, the 20250508 manual controls, and the draft tutorial/assembler sources do not override either specification [10].
